title: TA9-02715
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, herein called the claimant, seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the IRPA.1 Joined in this claim are her two minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX. Pursuant to section 167(2) of the IRPA, XXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXX is the designated representative of the minor claimants. I accept the claimants are nationals of Mexico.2 Allegations
The claimant alleges a well-founded fear of persecution and a risk of harm at the hands of her estranged husband, XXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXX, "herein known as XXXX".

The claimant began a common law relationship with XXXX in 1992 and bore two children in 1993 and 1997. Subsequently, the couple married on XXXXX, 2000. The claimant states in her narrative in paragraph two, "as the years went by he became very violent and a womanizer".3 The beatings and threats escalated after their marriage. The claimant alleges helplessness as XXXX threatened to kill the claimant and take the children away from her family. XXXX did not allow the claimant to have contact with her family. As their eldest, a son, became aware of the abuse, he rebelled and was hit by his father. In XXXX2007, the claimant sought help through DIF (System for Integral Family Development). XXXX was sent a notice to appear but did not, beating the claimant and then disappearing. In XXXX 2008, XXXX reappeared and beat the claimant who had to be hospitalized. He took the children for four days. After hospital release, XXXX continued to harass the claimant and still threatened to take the children away. The claimant filed a final report on XXXX, 2009 and travelled to Canada on XXXX, 2009 and made a refugee claim the next day. Determination

I find that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground, or that she would personally be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to her country. Therefore, I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.

The determinative issue in this case is whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In this regard, I considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Mexico, whether the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail herself of that protection, and whether she has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.
In making my determination, I have considered and applied the Gender Guidelines.4 ANALYSIS State Protection

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. Having canvassed the country conditions documents, I find that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. The country has an estimated 2,600 police forces with approximately 400,000 officers operating at the municipal, state, and federal levels. During the year the government deployed approximately 50,000 military in 10 states to support, and in some municipalities to coordinate, the fight against the country's well-armed and well-funded organized criminal groups. The government has continued its long-term effort to reform and improve the country's police organizations, with the goal of replacing the military in its domestic law enforcement function.5

To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens.6 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.7 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.8 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.9 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.10

Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.11 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.12

The claimant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.13 In a functioning democracy, a claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.14 The documentary evidence15 before the Board indicates that Mexico is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Therefore, in countries such as Mexico, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.16 Local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.17 No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.18 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.19

The Board finds that it would be unreasonable to expect in any society that all violent acts reported to police would result in immediate prosecutions or convictions. The Federal Court has held that a claimant's decision to flee before police have had an opportunity to properly respond to and investigate a transgression did not amount to a lack of state protection.20 In this particular case, there is no information to suggest that police were not making genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimant's allegations and apprehend the claimant's perpetrator. The claimant's choice to leave Mexico may have resulted in the investigation being delayed or stymied, given that she , as the victim, was a key witness.

Further, I considered the claimant's efforts to report any of this information to any other authority and find that the claimant did make two reports to the DIF who supported the claimant by involving the Attorney General's Office.

The Board accepts that Mexico has had some difficulties in the past with addressing the criminality and corruption that exist within the security forces in Mexico. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. I am of the view in canvassing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico.

Mexico is a democratic country, with functioning political and judicial systems and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens. Thus the burden on the claimant to seek protection from the state agencies of the country is a high one which she should have first attempted prior to seeking international protection.21 The state authorities do and will take steps to protect victims of crime and corruption. For example, documentary evidence22 indicates that the Mexican Government continues to push forward with federal police reform by focusing on rigorous new recruiting, training and vetting measures. The Federal Preventive Police (PFP) has internal regulations with disciplinary measures that classify transgressors and apply sanctions, including removal, suspension or dismissal.23 To enforce police internal rules, a collegiate organ, headed by Internal Affairs General Coordinator, decides whether there is responsibility or not. The Attorney General's Office (PGR) provides three offices to control its members (the Public Ministry and the Judicial Police). The three offices are: the Responsibility Control Centre, the General [inspector] and the Internal Accountability.24 The first office is in charge of testing the institution's public officials' adherence to legality, professionalism and impartiality. More importantly, the Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical, and a complainant can seek redress at a higher level if dissatisfied with the services at the local level. Reports about police misconduct or corruption can also made to the police complaints division of the Federal District's Ministry of Public Security.25 Furthermore, in the Federal District, individuals wishing to report police corruption can file a complaint with Internal Affairs or the Internal Controller of the Federal District Department of Public Security.26

The documentary27 evidence indicates that Mexico is not in a state of collapse, and further, has been making and continues to make serious efforts to fight crime and corruption. All 31 states in Mexico maintain a preventive and judicial police force. The judicial police are the law enforcement branch of the state level Public Ministry (MP), the Attorney General's Office (PGJ) is responsible for investigating and prosecuting local criminal offences, and the Federal Preventative Police (PFP) maintains order and security. The coordination for Federal Support Forces contains special operations and emergency response and the Regional Security Coordination supervises 34 regional commands. The military is responsible for external security but also has significant domestic security responsibilities, particularly in combating drug trafficking and maintaining order, a role that has been increased significantly over the years due to military training and the perception that it is relatively free of corruption. The country also has a number of other state agencies that address criminality, including drug trafficking, kidnapping and corruption in an effort to assist citizens to obtain state protection.

Although corruption is an ongoing problem in Mexico, anticorruption efforts continue. Under the Fox administration all agencies, departments and government institutions, including the Mexican military, were asked to adhere to strict enforcement of anticorruption measures. During 2007, the Calderon Administration strictly targeted corruption within the federal government. It is reported that each year, the underlying causes of corruption diminish, as better pay and benefits are provided, better selection criteria are employed for new employees, and more modern investigative techniques are applied. Documentary evidence indicates28 that the Mexican Government continues to push forward with federal police reform by focusing on rigorous new recruiting, training and vetting measures. There are government agencies in Mexico that assist citizens in lodging complaints regarding the conduct of state officials. For example, the Secretariat of Public Services (Secretaría de la Función Pública, SFP) offers various services to citizens wishing to report acts of corruption. Citizens may lodge complaints in person at the SFP offices or at the office of the Attorney General (PGR). There is also a Telephone Assistance System for Citizens (Sistema de Atención Telefónica a la Ciudadanía, SACTEL). The SACTEL has a 24-hour hotline service operating 365 days a year recording complaints made by citizens against public servants. Further documentary evidence indicates that persons seeking redress from corrupt or complicit officials can do so through the National or State Human Rights Commissions and the General Comptroller's Assistance Directorate. There is documentary evidence that persons who face police misconduct, inefficiency or corruption can ask the Program Against Impunity, or the Office of the Attorney General (PGR) to investigate federal and state police failures or misconduct. Similar to federal police forces, state offices of the Justice Attorney General usually have an internal affairs body that controls and evaluates complaints against its personnel. For example, the state Attorney General's office has had in place a general inspector since 1977 and this entity is tasked to control and evaluate the workings of public ministry and judicial police units. In June 2007, President Calderon purged 284 federal police commanders, including federal commanders of all 31 states and the federal district.29 These commanders were suspended and subjected to drug and polygraph tests. The Mexican government immediately named replacements for the 284 dismissed commanders. In late October 2008, an elite unit within the Federal Attorney General's office known as SEIDO was implicated in a scandal involving payoffs for sensitive information about anti-drug activities, with at least 35 officials and agents fired or arrested. In November of 2008, the former head of SIEDO, Noe Ramirez Mandujano, was arrested and accused of accepting bribes from a drug cartel. In October and November of 2008, two former heads of Interpol in Mexico were arrested for alleged ties to the Sinaloa cartel. In early December 2008, President Calderon stated that some 11,500 public employees had been sanctioned for corruption in the two years since he took office. In late May of 2009, the federal government made it's largest-ever arrest of politicians and senior officials in an anti-drug operation in the President's home state of Michoacan. Ten mayors and 18 other government and police officials, including state prosecutors and the heads of state and municipal police, were detained for alleged ties to the drug gangs.30 Federal police functions were restructured through the creation of the Federal Police (FP), an organization housed within the SSP. The FP was given new investigative powers by Congress, which will greatly increase the ability of federal law enforcement to confront Mexico's security challenges. The new force is being hired from a pool of vetted college graduates and trained in police procedures by U.S. and international instructors in San Luis Potosi. The preventative investigation function will be complemented by a national investigative police force in the reorganized Ministerial Federal Police belonging to the PGR. Under the new public security laws implemented in 2009, Federal Police are subject to greater vetting and hiring standards intended to assemble a force better able to combat the DTO's and become less susceptible to corruption31. A law on National Public Security, passed in January, mandated that within four years, Mexican law enforcement personnel at all levels undergo background checks to screen for possible corruption. The Secretariat of Public Security (SSP) has strengthened its vetting processes to review personnel and is working to establish a National Vetting Centre. Both current and prospective federal police officers will go through five layers of scrutiny: medical and anti-doping (toxicology) testing, polygraphs, and psychological and personal assets screening every six months. Since the beginning of the Calderon Administration, more than 11,000 federal public officials and police have been vetted, as well as an estimated 25,000 state and local public officials and police, and officials at the Customs and Migration Institute. Assistance under the Merida Initiative is supporting Mexican efforts here.32 The SSP is developing a National Police Registry to track security personnel by maintaining files with their biographic and biometric data. The first goal is to register all active Mexican police officers (federal, state, and local), auxiliary police officers, and private security companies in Mexico. Once completed, the system will contain the individual's photo, biographical data, 10 fingerprints, DNA samples, voice samples, and personal data (all employment related information, to include date of hire, education, training, disciplinary actions, and terminations). According to SSP, approximately 87 percent of Mexico's 473,693 active state and federal police officers have been registered, while approximately 35 percent of Mexico's 128,703 active state and federal private security personnel have been registered. The second goal of the project is to establish connectivity among all 2,500 federal, state, and municipal police agencies in Mexico. So far, 150 of Mexico's largest municipalities are connected to the registry, representing approximately 68 percent of Mexico's entire police force.33 The Government of Mexico has established an annual public security subsidy fund for the country's most crime-ridden municipalities. In 2008, 134 municipalities and 15 districts in the Federal District received resources under the subsidy, amounting to nearly 4.8 billion pesos. In order for municipalities to be eligible for the subsidy, they must adopt police practices that conform to those on the national level.34 During the year, the Calderon government undertook a number of actions to address corruption within the law enforcement community, including the greater use of polygraphs and background checks on law enforcement employees. While this vetting had some success at the federal level, it lagged behind at the state and municipal levels due to funding constraints and the large numbers of state and municipal officers. Additionally, the GOM made a number of high profile arrests to demonstrate its commitment to root out corruption across all levels of government. In May, raids in the state of Michoacan led to the arrest of ten mayors with alleged ties to corruption. Recent police and legal reforms appear to be making progress in the fight against corruption, but it is clear that more time and more reforms are required to make lasting progress.35 All these actions indicate that Mexico is making serious effort to combat corruption, abuse, and inefficiency in policing operations.

As a result of the changes to Mexican policing, Mexican law enforcement has advanced in the following areas: There has been a major and sustained increase in public security budgets allowing for improvements in equipment and technology; these investments have allowed for the strengthening of 066 (911) call centres and communications systems, and the purchase of vehicles, uniforms, bullet proof vests, guns and other tools necessary to professional police work; the federal government has a far greater law enforcement capacity than it had 15 years ago; there is consensus on the need to professionalize federal, state, and municipal law enforcement through better selection, improved training, better remuneration, and improved operational procedures rather than simply limiting officer discretion; this consensus has been enshrined in law and the federal government has provided funding to help states and municipalities comply with the law; there has been a dramatic and impressive increase in the use of vetting, including polygraph tests; the SSP conducted 54,536 trust evaluations over the course of one year, including 24,971 applicants, 3,878 federal personnel, and 25,687 state and municipal police; institutional mechanisms (e.g. National Public Security Council), communication systems (i.e. Platform Mexico), and databases (e.g. registry of law enforcement personnel) have been created to allow for (but not guarantee) better coordination between Mexico's police forces.

With respect to efforts to combat violence against women, Mexico has enacted civil, administrative and criminal legislation which prohibits gender-related violence and as such, have enacted sentences which include fines and detention.36 Approved by the Senate in December 2006 and enacted as federal legislation by President Felipe Calderon on 1 February 2007, the General Law on Women's Access to a Life Free of Violence (Ley General de Acceso de las Mujeres a un Vida Libre de Violencia) (IPS 14 Feb. 2007) requires "federal and local authorities to prevent, punish and eradicate violence against women."37 The Mexican government has ratified all international instruments to fulfill women's rights, end inequality and eradicate gender based violence. Legislative reforms enacted at federal and state levels over the past 10 years have begun to give weight to these international commitments, as have increased training of officials and investment to improve access to justice and information on women's rights. Nevertheless, levels of violence remain high and the real impact of many official initiatives has yet to become apparent. The women's movement in Mexico has been at the forefront of efforts to raise awareness of the high levels of gender based violence. It has been instrumental in bringing the issue to the attention of the Mexican government and tracking the record of authority's prevention and punishment record. This has resulted in an increased acknowledgement by authorities that they have a responsibility to take action.38

As of 29 January 2009, 30 out of 32 states have passed the law in Mexico; however, there remain a number of states that have not realized key provisions, including "implementation mechanisms," an agency coordination mechanism, and the building of new shelters. Nevertheless, according to the ex-legislator and co-creator of the General Law, Angélica de la Peña Gómez, the law has been successful for two reasons: the first because it has been able to gain approval in almost every state in the country, and "broke the inertia" other national laws have faced in state congresses; and the second concerns the approval of budgetary payments of 3 million pesos [$1 CAN = 10.62 MEX (Canada 22 Apr. 2009)] for each state to implement the law. The legal coordinator of the National Institute for Women (Instituto Nacional de las Mujeres, INMUJERES), also describes the General Law as a "very significant advance" because 30 states have passed it.

However, sustained funding at the state and local level remains an issue. Various news and human rights sources report that two years after the enactment of the General Law on Women's Access to a Life Free of Violence (Ley General de Acceso de las Mujeres a una Vida Libre de Violencia), the law continues to face implementation challenges. Freedom House notes that since the General Law was passed in February 2007, "its efficacy has yet to be determined" (2008). 39

When looking at the totality of the Board's documents, one must consider some of the dismal reports concerning Mexico's efforts to protect women against violence. A summary prepared by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), reports that in Mexico, the investigation, as well as the punishment, of violence against women is scarce or absent, and that officials lack both awareness and training on the issue. El Universal reports that even though campaigns promoting denunciations against "crimes" have been launched, there are insufficient services to protect and attend to victims and that local and federal "public employees and authorities" are inefficient in carrying out their responsibilities in the investigation of cases of violence against women and "continue to demonstrate serious acts of negligence, omission and crimes in the administration of justice".40

Even with this record, there is also evidence that Mexico is taking measures to combat crimes against women. The law criminalizes rape, including spousal rape, and imposes penalties of up to 20 years' imprisonment. It is acknowledged that rape victims rarely filed complaints with police, in part because of the authorities' ineffective and unsupportive responses to victims, the victims' fear of publicity, and a perception that prosecution of cases was unlikely. Even so, according to the government's cabinet-level National Institute of Women (INMUJERES), 3,687 men were convicted nationwide for rape and an additional 4,467 were in pre-trial detention for rape. FEVIMTRA, staffed by 19 legal, administrative and technical support professionals is responsible for leading government programs to combat domestic violence and trafficking in persons. Its work includes prosecuting the crimes, raising awareness with potential victims and government officials. The low staffing creates challenges in moving from investigation to conviction. IMUJERES reported its national hotline established under The National Plan for a Life Without Violence received 19,595 calls during the year. There are some government run shelters while civil society and women's groups maintain most available shelters.41

It is conceded that Mexico's track record regarding its efforts to combat violence against women has been poor. However, there has been some progress in establishing legislation and institutions to particularly address the needs of family and gender violence. One of the underlying causes of a failure to address the violence against women in the family is the widespread belief that it is a private matter which should be resolved within the family. Amnesty International believes Mexico has made some important advances in recent years in defending women's rights. In particular, human rights standards have been incorporated into national and state laws. However, there remains a need to bridge the gap between legislation and implementation.42 It is in this gap, between enacting legislation, and the implementation of that legislation, where the adequacy of state protection for victims of family or gender violence must be determined. Not only this, but each individual case must be determined on its own merits, taking into account the particular circumstances relating to this claimant.

Despite what all of the documentary evidence says, what actually happened in this particular case? Although the claimant began a relationship with XXXX in 1992 and indicates the abuse escalated after their marriage in 2000, the claimant did not seek protection from authorities until XXXX 2007. The claimant also indicated that XXXX began to abuse his children in 2005. The claimant explained the long delay in seeking protection was due to the fear and threats of XXXX even though the claimant testified she believed the police would help her. XXXX was sent a notice to appear by the authorities but disappeared until XXXX 2008. When he returned, he beat the claimant so badly she required hospitalization. XXXX also took the children for four days. The claimant did not report this beating to the authorities out of fear as she felt the authorities had let her down in 2007 when they did nothing.

I reject the claimant's explanation as providing proof that the police were ineffective. The claimant was accepted by DIF and the police authorities were involved. XXXX disappeared for nine moths and then the claimant did not report a further serious beating upon his return. The authorities did respond to the claimant's denunciation and sent a notice to XXXX who disappeared. The claimant views this as a lack of help from the authorities while I view this as an attempt to help the claimant by the police authorities. I accept the claimant is not satisfied by the authorities' lack of success, especially in light of the circumstances in XXXX 2008 when she was beaten again and the claimant failed to report to an authority. I am not persuaded by the claimant that there is a lack of state protection.

Further, the claimant did file one more denunciation with the help of DIF on XXXX, 2009, four months after the XXXX 2008 beating which hospitalized the claimant. This denunciation was made only twelve days prior to the claimant's departure for Canada. The claimant speculates the police did nothing as XXXX bribed the police, "I suspected". The claimant further indicates that the police did nothing as she saw him after her XXXX, 2009 denunciation. I asked the claimant if she followed up or made further reports of harassment to the police. The claimant replied she did not as she planned to leave (Mexico), "so I didn't want to do anything about it". I accept the claimant did make a minimal effort to secure police protection but I am not persuaded it was a reasonable effort as the claimant did not report the XXXX 2008 beating when XXXX returned after his disappearance as he had evaded the notice to appear delivered by hand in XXXX, 2007.43 Given that the claimant is a victim of gender related violence, I have considered the Chairperson's Guideline 7,44 and accept some mitigating circumstances by the claimant in seeking state protection. Nevertheless, the claimant has demonstrated she is able to seek state protection. As such, I do not accept her two advances to the state to prove a lack of state protection. The claimant made a final denunciation only twelve days before her departure to Canada and four months after her severe beating. The claimant has not given the state authorities a reasonable opportunity to investigate the beating as her wounds, which could be used as evidence had healed by then. The claimant also admits that she really was not interested in pursuing the XXXX, 2009 denunciation as she knew she was leaving Mexico soon. The police have not been given a legitimate opportunity to investigate the actions of XXXX as the one person who should support the police at first delayed in initiating this denunciation for four months and then left Mexico only days after the denunciation was made. Without a viable witness or evidence, the police's ability to investigate and prosecute would be negated.

In view of these principles, I find that the claimant has not provided the requisite clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Mexico is inadequate. The claimant did go to the police in 2007 and 2009. Both times, DIF supported her needs and the Attorney General's office interceded. The Board finds that it would be unreasonable to expect in any society that all violent acts reported to police would result in immediate prosecutions or convictions. The Federal Court has held that a claimant's decision to flee before police have had an opportunity to properly respond to and investigate a transgression did not amount to a lack of state protection.45 In this particular case, there is no information to suggest that police were not making genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimant's allegations. In fact, based on the claimant's testimony, the Mexican authorities did respond.

I find that the claimant's decision to flee Mexico during the initial stages of the police investigation from the XXXX 2009 denunciation seriously undermines her credibility relating to her efforts to seek state protection in the context of rebutting the presumption of state protection in Mexico.

Regarding counsel's submissions, I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation to indicate that inefficiency, bribery and corruption remain issues in Mexican security forces at all levels, as well as within the public service sector. It is accepted that victims of domestic violence do face hurdles when seeking redress through the justice system. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the serious problem of domestic abuse and gender violence in that country. The objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of domestic and gender violence, that Mexico is making serious efforts to address the problem, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims.

Therefore, having considered the totality of the evidence, I find that the claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and that the claimant did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances to avail herself of that protection before making a claim for refugee protection. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of Mexico would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it.

For all these reasons, I find that that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the Act, as state protection is available to her. As the claims of her two minor children are joined to her claim, they must also fail.
I determine that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims. (signed) "C. Wedgbury" C.
